opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the intuition comes from how we think about memory consolidation in the brain. During the day you take in a lot of new information, and it gets stored quickly in a fast, somewhat fragile system. During sleep, that information gets replayed and gradually moved into longer-term storage, where it's integrated with everything you already know.

In the paper, model A is the one actively interacting with the world, picking up new information in context or in its fast-adapting memory. Model B is where that knowledge eventually gets consolidated into the weights. The problem is that if you keep pushing new knowledge into a fixed set of parameters, you hit a capacity issue. You're overwriting things, and that's where catastrophic forgetting comes from. The new knowledge competes with the old knowledge for the same space.

So adding parameters to model B is a way of giving the consolidation process somewhere to put things. Rather than forcing the model to squeeze new information into weights already doing important work, you expand its capacity so it can absorb the new knowledge while preserving what it already had. It's a bit like how memory isn't purely a fixed-size container. There's structural change happening when you learn and consolidate.

There's also a practical side. We don't want to grow parameters every time the model sees one new fact. That would be wasteful and wouldn't scale. The idea is that you accumulate experience during the "wake" phase, and then in the "sleep" phase you do this more deliberate consolidation step, which is where it makes sense to allocate new capacity and distill what was learned into it.

The broader point is that continual learning probably isn't just about better optimization tricks on a fixed architecture. At some point you need to think about the memory system itself: how much it can hold, how knowledge moves between levels, and when it's worth expanding. Adding parameters to model B is one concrete way of taking that seriously.

r001.rationale: The response says that expanding model B gives it capacity to absorb new knowledge without squeezing it into existing weights.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so that's actually one of the design choices we went back and forth on the most, so I'm glad you asked about it.

The setup, just to ground it, is that we have two phases that mirror what the brain does. There's a "wake" phase where the model is actively interacting with the world, taking in new information, updating a fast memory. And then there's a "sleep" phase, where the model stops taking in new input and instead replays and consolidates what it saw during the day into its longer-term weights. Model A is essentially the awake model, and model B is the one doing the consolidation.

Now, the naive thing to do would be to say, okay, during sleep just take all those memories and fine-tune them into the same parameters you already have. And when we tried that, we ran into two problems. The first is the classic one, catastrophic forgetting. You push the new experiences into the pretrained weights and you start degrading the general knowledge the model came in with. The second problem is more subtle, which is that there's just not enough free capacity. A pretrained model's parameters are already doing a lot of work. If you keep consolidating new memories day after day into the same fixed set of weights, you eventually saturate. There's nowhere for the new information to go without displacing something else.

So adding parameters to B is really about giving the consolidation process somewhere to write. You can think of it a bit like growing new connections. The brain doesn't learn by rewriting its existing synapses from scratch every night, it strengthens and forms new ones. So in model B we add a set of parameters whose job is specifically to absorb what came in during wake, and the sleep phase trains those while the core model stays largely protected. It decouples "what I knew before" from "what I learned recently," and then over time those recently learned things can become part of the longer-term structure.

There's also a practical angle. Because the added parameters are relatively small compared to the full model, the sleep phase is cheap. You're not doing a full fine-tune every cycle. And it makes the whole thing much more stable, because you can tell exactly what changed and, if a sleep cycle went badly, you can roll it back without touching the base.

So the short version is, the extra parameters are what make sleep a constructive process instead of a destructive one. Without them, consolidation is just overwriting. With them, it's actually accumulation.

r001.rationale: It explains that B’s added parameters provide somewhere to store and absorb information acquired during wake, addressing the lack of capacity in the existing weights.

astra-6.text: The idea is to give model B additional capacity to absorb new information without having to overwrite what the model already knows. If you keep the capacity fixed, the same parameters have to serve both purposes: preserving old knowledge and fitting new experiences. That creates interference. Adding parameters gives us room for that new learning, and the sleep phase is then about consolidating what was learned into the model. So the extra parameters provide capacity; they don’t, by themselves, solve the consolidation problem.

r001.rationale: It says adding parameters gives model B room to absorb and fit new information, providing capacity for new learning.

sol-6.1.text: The idea is to give model B extra capacity to absorb new information without having to overwrite what the model already knows. If you keep the capacity fixed, learning something new can interfere with previously learned knowledge—that’s the catastrophic forgetting problem. The additional parameters give us room for that new learning, and then the sleep phase lets us consolidate it back into model A. So we separate acquiring new knowledge from integrating it into the existing model.

r001.rationale: It says the extra capacity lets model B absorb new information and gives it room for new learning.
